About this playbook

How this site is curated

Agents help keep this playbook current by finding new practices, writing updates and reviewing existing articles. Every content change still needs a human to review and approve the pull request.

The curation loop

Scouting finds possible additions, while peer review and source monitoring identify changes to existing articles. These findings enter the same backlog. The writer assesses their value, prepares useful changes with the right context and standards, and submits them for human approval.

Why agents maintain this playbook

Developing products with AI is an emerging practice. New methods, models and frameworks give teams more approaches to assess and try. Keeping a playbook useful means finding relevant developments, checking their evidence and revisiting earlier advice.

A wholly manual process takes substantial research and editorial time and can struggle to keep up. This playbook uses agents to carry out that recurring work, so people can focus their attention on the proposed changes and the evidence behind them.

The maintenance process follows a light factory approach: agents prepare and check changes, and a person reviews them before publication. The aim is current, useful guidance with an accountable human approval decision.

The writer follows shared standards

A note on AI-written content

A Hermes-powered writer agent drafts and maintains this playbook under human editorial oversight.

We apologise for any passages that sound unnatural or lack clarity. The agent will continue refining the content through source verification, peer feedback and human review to improve its clarity and natural flow.

The writer uses two repository standards to guide the content, its flow and the checks before a change is submitted:

  • The writing standard (writing.md) starts with the reader’s task. It calls for plain British English, connected explanations, consistent terminology and concrete actions with named owners and expected results. Its editorial acceptance checklist covers evidence, coherence, attribution, useful next steps and the distinction between requirements, recommendations and examples.
  • The design standard (design.md) guides reading width, typography, navigation, page maps, tables and accessible diagrams. It distinguishes topic explanations from worked examples and includes an acceptance checklist for responsive layouts, keyboard access, contrast, reduced motion and print readability.

The writer is required to research and reference established practices online. It does not invent new theories or methodologies. Every article that presents a methodology or framework must link directly to its original source and explain any adaptation made for this guide. Source notes belong in the article’s final Sources section, with precise inline links where needed to connect a claim to its evidence.

Before submitting a change, the writer rereads the affected explanation and surrounding material against the writing checklist, then checks the page against the design checklist. Review records distinguish what was checked from what remains uncertain.

Scouts assess what deserves attention

Content scouting agents powered by Muse, Hermes and OpenAI scan online for recent practices and materials that could improve the playbook. They compare each candidate article with the existing content using three questions:

  • Novelty: Does it introduce relevant content that the playbook does not already cover?
  • Enrichment and gap coverage: Does it resolve an omission, deepen an explanation or provide stronger evidence for existing guidance?
  • Loss if missed: What would readers lose if the material were not covered, and how consequential would that omission be?

The assessment produces a criticality score and a low, medium or high priority, supported by the reasons for that judgement. Medium- and high-priority findings are filed as issues in the issue backlog for consideration. An issue records a candidate for review; it is not a commitment to include the material.

From issue to approved change

The writer scans the backlog and takes high-priority issues for review. Criticality identifies what needs attention; the writer then assesses whether the proposed change would add enough value for readers.

If the evidence, scope or instructions are unclear, the writer asks a human for clarification via Telegram. The writer records the response with the issue and uses it as context before continuing the affected work. Clarification does not replace pull-request approval.

  1. Review the evidence and value. Read the original material, compare it with the affected pages and assess the benefit, overlap and effort of the proposed change. Record the decision and its reasons on the issue.
  2. Implement changes with high assessed value. Prepare the update on a feature branch, retain direct source references and check the revised content and presentation against the shared standards.
  3. Submit a pull request. Describe the resulting change, link the issue and sources, and report the checks performed and any unresolved questions.
  4. Obtain human approval. A human reviewer examines the change and its evidence, requests revisions where needed and decides whether to approve it. Every content change requires this approval before it is merged and published.

Agent checks and peer-review scores support the human decision. They do not authorise publication.

Keep references current and publish one page-wide check date

Source-monitoring agents powered by Hermes and OpenAI are required to check all online references regularly. Each sourced article must have one final Sources section, with exactly one page-wide “References last checked” date immediately after its Sources heading and one numbered source list. Keep per-source outcomes, check dates and history in reference-checks.json, not as competing dates in source entries. The page-wide date records the maintenance pass; it does not guarantee that sources have remained unchanged or that every claim has been verified.

The check covers whether the destination is accessible, whether it still supports the cited claim and whether a newer version changes the guidance. The agent records the source URL, check date, result, scope and any unresolved limitation in the inventory. Broken links, changed claims and sources that cannot be verified become maintenance findings for review. Retain partial or unverified scope limitations in the applicable source entry as well as in the inventory.

A working link alone does not establish that an article is accurate. Do not advance the page-wide date from a partial check: record that check’s outcome and history in the inventory, retain the existing page-wide date and publish the remaining scope limitation. A complete page maintenance pass may retain an inaccessible or unverified source, but must state that limitation rather than imply blanket verification.

Peer review improves articles and standards

A separate group of reviewer agents powered by Muse and OpenAI examines existing articles paragraph by paragraph. Each paragraph receives a score from 1 to 10 for each of three qualities: how natural it sounds, how easy it is to understand and how accurately it represents the evidence. Higher scores indicate a stronger result.

Reviewers file issues that identify the passage, explain the problem and propose an improvement. Scores help direct attention, while the explanation and source evidence give the writer something concrete to assess. An agent’s readability score does not establish that a reader has understood the article.

The writer reviews these issues and assesses the value of the proposed correction before changing the article. For an accepted improvement, the order is deliberate: correct the content first, then examine whether the standards also need refinement. A writing or design rule may itself have contributed to the problem.

The writer rechecks the corrected passage and its surrounding explanation, then considers whether a change to writing.md or design.md would help prevent the same problem elsewhere. Article corrections and any proposed standard changes go through pull requests with human approval.

Help improve the playbook. If an explanation is awkward, unclear or out of date, raise an issue with the page link, the affected passage and what would make it more useful.
